```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(20260824)

C = {
    "blue":   "#2c6e9b",
    "orange": "#d1743a",
    "green":  "#4f8f63",
    "red":    "#b5483d",
    "grey":   "#9aa3ab",
    "dark":   "#2c4a63",
}

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 130,
    "font.size": 9,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})


def correlated_X(N, p, rng):
    """N units, p covariates, with a non-trivial correlation structure."""
    A = rng.normal(size=(p, p))
    Sig = A @ A.T + np.eye(p)
    d = np.sqrt(np.diag(Sig))
    Sig = Sig / np.outer(d, d)
    return rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(p), Sig, size=N)


def pair_distances(X):
    """Squared Mahalanobis distance between every pair of units.

    Whitening first turns the quadratic form into a plain squared Euclidean
    distance, which lets the whole matrix be built in one vectorised step.
    """
    Si = np.linalg.inv(np.cov(X, rowvar=False, bias=True))
    Z = X @ np.linalg.cholesky(Si).T.T
    return ((Z[:, None, :] - Z[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1), Si


def optimal_pairs(d2):
    """Minimum-weight perfect matching on the complete graph (blossom)."""
    N = d2.shape[0]
    G = nx.Graph()
    for i in range(N):
        for j in range(i + 1, N):
            G.add_edge(i, j, weight=d2[i, j])
    return np.array([tuple(e) for e in nx.min_weight_matching(G)])


def greedy_pairs(d2):
    """Repeatedly take the closest remaining available pair."""
    N = d2.shape[0]
    d = d2.astype(float).copy()
    np.fill_diagonal(d, np.inf)
    out = []
    for _ in range(N // 2):
        i, j = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(d), d.shape)
        out.append((int(i), int(j)))
        d[[i, j], :] = np.inf
        d[:, [i, j]] = np.inf
    return np.array(out)
```

You have a few hundred units and you want two halves that look alike.
[Rerandomization](../rerandomization/) reaches that by discarding splits that
come out badly balanced. Pairwise matching reaches it by construction. Pair
every unit with its closest counterpart in covariate space, then flip a coin
inside each pair. Each arm then holds exactly one unit from every pair, so the
two halves are matched unit by unit rather than only on average.

This article answers three questions. Does matching gain you more than
rerandomization? Why does the pairing step have to be solved properly? And how
do you analyse the experiment afterwards?

## What it does

Closeness between two units is measured with the
[Mahalanobis distance](../mahalanobis-distance/), which avoids double-counting
correlated covariates. With $N$ units and $k$ covariates:

::: {.keybox}
1. Compute the covariate covariance matrix $S$ **once**, from all $N$ units.
2. For every pair of units $i$ and $j$, compute the squared distance between
   them:
   $$ D^2(i,j) \;=\; (x_i - x_j)^{\!\top} S^{-1} (x_i - x_j). $$
3. Choose the $N/2$ pairs that **minimise the total within-pair distance**,
   subject to covering every unit exactly once.
4. Inside each pair, flip a coin to decide which unit goes to treatment.
:::

Step 2 is the same quadratic form as in the Mahalanobis article, applied to the
gap between two units instead of the gap between a unit and the mean.
Everything from there carries over: affine invariance, correlated columns
counted once, and the one-hot-with-a-baseline or pseudo-inverse treatment of
categorical covariates.

Step 4 is what keeps this a randomised experiment. Each pair contributes one
independent coin flip, so a sample of $N$ units has $2^{N/2}$ possible
assignments. At $N = 400$ that is about $1.6 \times 10^{60}$. Assigning
deterministically within pairs, say the higher-spending unit always to control,
would leave a single possible split and no basis for a $p$-value.

Step 3 is the part that goes wrong in practice.

## The pairing is an optimisation problem, not a sorting problem

The obvious way to form pairs is greedy. Take the two closest units anywhere in
the sample, set them aside as a pair, then repeat on what is left. It is short
to write and it does not produce the minimum.

```{python}
#| label: fig-greedy
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: 'Forty units, two covariates, each line joining a matched pair. Greedy matching takes the closest available pair at each step, so it spends the dense middle of the sample first and leaves the units at the edges to pair with whatever remains.'

Xd = correlated_X(40, 2, np.random.default_rng(11))
d2d, _ = pair_distances(Xd)
po_d, pg_d = optimal_pairs(d2d), greedy_pairs(d2d)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, prs, name in [(axes[0], po_d, "Optimal"), (axes[1], pg_d, "Greedy")]:
    worst = max(range(len(prs)), key=lambda m: d2d[prs[m][0], prs[m][1]])
    for m, (i, j) in enumerate(prs):
        hot = (m == worst)
        ax.plot(Xd[[i, j], 0], Xd[[i, j], 1],
                color=C["red"] if hot else C["dark"],
                lw=2.0 if hot else 1.1, zorder=3 if hot else 2,
                alpha=1.0 if hot else 0.75)
    ax.scatter(Xd[:, 0], Xd[:, 1], s=16, color=C["blue"], zorder=4)
    tot = sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in prs)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\ntotal $D^2$ = {tot:.1f}, "
                 f"worst pair = {d2d[prs[worst][0], prs[worst][1]]:.1f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("$x_2$")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

demo = {
    "mult": (sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in pg_d)
             / sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)),
    "worst": (max(d2d[i, j] for i, j in pg_d)
              / max(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)),
}
```

The worst pair is highlighted in each panel. Greedy matching strands the units
it leaves until last, and a stranded pair is a pair whose covariate gap the coin
flip cannot undo. That gap goes straight into the variance of the treatment
effect estimate, so the tail of the distance distribution matters more than its
total.

How much greedy costs depends on the sample. Forty units is a hard case for it,
and it runs up `{python} f"{demo['mult']:.1f}"` times the total distance and
`{python} f"{demo['worst']:.0f}"` times the worst pair. At a few hundred units
the totals come much closer together, while the worst pair stays several times
further apart.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-greedy
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'Optimal against greedy pairing on the same samples. Greedy loses some of the total, and much more of the worst case.'

rows = []
for N, p in [(100, 4), (200, 4), (200, 8)]:
    Xg = correlated_X(N, p, np.random.default_rng(100 + N + p))
    d2g, _ = pair_distances(Xg)
    po, pg = optimal_pairs(d2g), greedy_pairs(d2g)
    to = sum(d2g[i, j] for i, j in po)
    tg = sum(d2g[i, j] for i, j in pg)
    mo = max(d2g[i, j] for i, j in po)
    mg = max(d2g[i, j] for i, j in pg)
    rows.append({
        "Sample": f"N = {N}, k = {p}",
        "Total D<sup>2</sup>, optimal": f"{to:.1f}",
        "Total D<sup>2</sup>, greedy": f"{tg:.1f} (+{100 * (tg / to - 1):.0f}%)",
        "Worst pair, optimal": f"{mo:.2f}",
        "Worst pair, greedy": f"{mg:.2f} ({mg / mo:.1f}×)",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).style.hide(axis="index")
```

The correct problem is a minimum-weight perfect matching on a general graph.
Every unit is a vertex, every pair of units is an edge weighted by $D^2(i,j)$,
and you want the cheapest set of edges that touches each vertex once. Edmonds'
blossom algorithm solves it exactly in $O(N^3)$.

Two points of confusion are worth clearing up. First, this is not the
assignment problem, and the Hungarian algorithm does not apply. That algorithm
matches one set to a different set, treated units to control units. Here there
is a single pool and any unit may pair with any other, so the graph is not
bipartite. Greevy et al. (2004) introduced the non-bipartite version for exactly
this design. Second, the problem is solved rather than approximated, so there
is no tuning to do and no reason to settle for greedy. In Python it is one call
in `networkx`; in R it is the `nbpMatching` package.

## Does it gain more than rerandomization?

Both designs are aiming at the same thing, so the comparison is worth making
directly. The table below fixes one sample of 400 units with four covariates,
then repeats the assignment 4,000 times under each design and measures how much
the estimate moves around.

```{python}
#| label: headtohead-setup
#| include: false

N, p, REPS = 400, 4, 4000
rng_h = np.random.default_rng(7)

Xh = correlated_X(N, p, rng_h)
d2h, Sih = pair_distances(Xh)
pairs = optimal_pairs(d2h)
assert len(pairs) == N // 2 and len(set(pairs.ravel())) == N
i0, i1 = pairs[:, 0], pairs[:, 1]
nP = len(pairs)

# ---- three designs, each drawn once and reused for both outcome models -----
T_cr = np.zeros((REPS, N), bool)
for b in range(REPS):
    T_cr[b, rng_h.permutation(N)[: N // 2]] = True

a_thr = stats.chi2.ppf(0.01, p)
T_rr = np.zeros((REPS, N), bool)
tries = 0
for b in range(REPS):
    while True:
        t = np.zeros(N, bool)
        t[rng_h.permutation(N)[: N // 2]] = True
        tries += 1
        dbar = Xh[t].mean(0) - Xh[~t].mean(0)
        if (N / 4) * dbar @ Sih @ dbar <= a_thr:
            T_rr[b] = t
            break

coin = rng_h.random((REPS, nP)) < 0.5
T_pm = np.zeros((REPS, N), bool)
T_pm[np.repeat(np.arange(REPS), nP),
     np.where(coin, i0[None, :], i1[None, :]).ravel()] = True

# ---- two outcome models, same covariates, same total signal strength ------
# The models are built to share R^2 overall while differing sharply in how
# much of that signal a linear function of the covariates can reach.
beta = np.array([1.0, 0.6, -0.8, 0.4])
Xi_h = np.column_stack([np.ones(N), Xh])


def make_y(kind, rng):
    if kind == "linear":
        sig = Xh @ beta
    else:
        sig = (2.0 * np.sin(2.2 * Xh[:, 0])
               + 1.5 * (Xh[:, 1] > 0.3) * Xh[:, 2]
               + 0.9 * Xh[:, 0] * Xh[:, 1]
               + 0.8 * Xh[:, 3] ** 2)
    sig = sig / sig.std() * 1.4
    y = sig + rng.normal(0, 1.0, N)
    # The linear share projects the signal, not the outcome, onto X. Projecting
    # the outcome would let OLS fit some of the noise and could push the linear
    # share above the total.
    lin = Xi_h @ np.linalg.lstsq(Xi_h, sig, rcond=None)[0]
    return y, sig.var() / y.var(), lin.var() / y.var()


def est_sd(T, y):
    mt = np.where(T, y[None, :], np.nan)
    mc = np.where(T, np.nan, y[None, :])
    return (np.nanmean(mt, 1) - np.nanmean(mc, 1)).std(ddof=1)


a_th = stats.chi2.ppf(0.01, p)
v_a = stats.chi2.cdf(a_th, p + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_th, p)

h2h, R2 = [], {}
for kind in ["linear", "nonlinear"]:
    y_k, r2_tot, r2_lin = make_y(kind, np.random.default_rng(3))
    base = est_sd(T_cr, y_k)
    rr = (est_sd(T_rr, y_k) / base) ** 2
    pm = (est_sd(T_pm, y_k) / base) ** 2
    R2[kind] = dict(tot=r2_tot, lin=r2_lin, rr=rr, pm=pm)
    h2h.append({
        "Outcome model": ("Linear in the covariates" if kind == "linear"
                          else "Non-linear in the covariates"),
        "R<sup>2</sup>, any function of X": f"{r2_tot:.2f}",
        "R<sup>2</sup>, linear in X": f"{r2_lin:.2f}",
        "Rerandomization, p<sub>a</sub> = 1%": f"{rr:.2f}",
        "Pairwise matching": f"{pm:.2f}",
    })
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-headtohead
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'Variance of the difference in means, as a fraction of the variance under plain randomisation. Lower is better. One fixed sample of 400 units and four covariates, 4,000 assignments under each design. The two outcome models carry the same total signal and differ in how much of it is linear.'

pd.DataFrame(h2h).style.hide(axis="index")
```

The two $R^2$ columns explain the result. Both outcome models leave the
same share of variance unexplained once you allow any function of the
covariates, so both offer the same gain in principle. They differ in how
much of that signal a *linear* function of the covariates can reach:
`{python} f"{R2['linear']['lin']:.2f}"` against
`{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['lin']:.2f}"`.

That column is the one rerandomization is limited by. A threshold on $M$
constrains the difference in covariate *means*, which pins down the linear
part of the response and leaves the rest untouched. Matching is limited by
the other column. The two units in a pair sit close together in covariate
space, so any function of the covariates takes nearly the same value on
each side of the coin flip, whether that function is linear or not.
Matching therefore performs about the same in both rows, while
rerandomization collapses from `{python} f"{R2['linear']['rr']:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['rr']:.2f}"`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Checking both numbers against theory

The variance ratio under rerandomization is $1 - (1 - v_a)R^2$, with $v_a$
the shrinkage factor from the
[rerandomization article](../rerandomization/) and $R^2$ the linear one. At
$k =$ `{python} f"{p}"` and $p_a = 1\%$, $v_a =$
`{python} f"{v_a:.3f}"`, so the formula predicts
`{python} f"{1 - (1 - v_a) * R2['linear']['lin']:.2f}"` for the linear
model against `{python} f"{R2['linear']['rr']:.2f}"` measured, and
`{python} f"{1 - (1 - v_a) * R2['nonlinear']['lin']:.2f}"` for the
non-linear model against `{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['rr']:.2f}"`
measured. Splitting the outcome into its linear fit and the residual shows
the mechanism directly: under rerandomization the variance of the fitted
part shrinks by a factor of about $v_a$, and the variance of the residual
part does not move.

For matching, a perfectly matched sample would reduce the variance to the
share of outcome variance the covariates do not explain, which is
$1 - R^2 =$ `{python} f"{1 - R2['nonlinear']['tot']:.2f}"` here against
`{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['pm']:.2f}"` achieved. The shortfall is the
price of pairs that are close but not identical.

The two designs differ in what you can do about a disappointing number.
Tightening the threshold drives $v_a$ towards zero, so rerandomization has
a dial. Matching has none: the within-pair distances are a property of the
sample, and once the matching is optimal there is nothing further to spend.
What limits it is covariate density, which is why matching improves as $N$
grows and degrades as $k$ grows.
:::

Bruhn and McKenzie (2009) reached a compatible conclusion from a different
direction. Surveying development field experiments, they report that at samples
of 300 or more the common designs balance future outcomes about equally well,
and that pairwise matching and stratification come out ahead in smaller samples
and for highly persistent outcomes. Their rerandomization comparison is to
rerandomization as commonly practised, with few covariates and a loose
threshold.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which to reach for

Matching is the safer default when you cannot describe the outcome as roughly
linear in the covariates, and when the sample is small enough that a few
awkward units could land on one side. Rerandomization is the better fit when the
covariates enter the response roughly linearly, when you want a dial you can
tighten, and when the pairing cannot survive to the analysis stage. The next
section covers that last condition, which is easy to overlook.
:::

## Odd numbers, and units with nothing close to them

A perfect matching needs an even $N$ and tolerates no exceptions, so two
practical cases need handling.

For odd $N$, or to drop units that match badly, add **sinks**. A sink is a
phantom unit placed at distance zero from every real unit and at infinite
distance from other sinks. Whichever real unit gets matched to a sink is
excluded from the experiment. One sink absorbs an odd unit. Adding $m$ sinks
excludes the $m$ units that were most expensive to pair, which is the cleanest
way to exclude the units whose matches would have been worst.

A **caliper** sets a maximum acceptable within-pair distance. Implementing it
by raising the weight of long edges can leave a problem with no feasible
solution, so the usual route is a caliper enforced through sinks: make a sink
cheaper than any pairing beyond the cap, and units with no acceptable partner
drop out by themselves. Every unit you exclude narrows what the experiment
covers, so record how many and which ones.

## Analysing a matched experiment

The point estimate needs no special treatment. Averaging the within-pair
differences and taking the plain difference in group means are the same
arithmetic, because every pair puts one unit in each arm. There is no way to
forget the matching when forming the estimate.

The standard error is a different matter.

```{python}
#| label: se-setup
#| include: false

y_nl, r2_nl, _ = make_y("nonlinear", np.random.default_rng(3))

Y = y_nl[None, :] + 0.0 * T_pm
mt = np.where(T_pm, Y, np.nan)
mc = np.where(T_pm, np.nan, Y)
est_pm = np.nanmean(mt, 1) - np.nanmean(mc, 1)
vt = np.nanvar(mt, 1, ddof=1)
vc = np.nanvar(mc, 1, ddof=1)
se_unpaired = np.sqrt(vt / (N // 2) + vc / (N // 2))

first_is_t = T_pm[:, i0]
wdiff = np.where(first_is_t, Y[:, i0] - Y[:, i1], Y[:, i1] - Y[:, i0])
se_paired = wdiff.std(1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(nP)

tc_un = stats.t.ppf(0.975, N - 2)
tc_pr = stats.t.ppf(0.975, nP - 1)
cov_un = (np.abs(est_pm) <= tc_un * se_unpaired).mean()
cov_pr = (np.abs(est_pm) <= tc_pr * se_paired).mean()

sd_true = est_pm.std(ddof=1)

se_tbl = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Quantity": "True spread of the estimate across assignments",
     "Value": f"{sd_true:.4f}", "95% CI coverage": ""},
    {"Quantity": "Reported SE, two-sample <i>t</i>-test",
     "Value": f"{se_unpaired.mean():.4f}",
     "95% CI coverage": f"{100 * cov_un:.1f}%"},
    {"Quantity": "Reported SE, within-pair differences",
     "Value": f"{se_paired.mean():.4f}",
     "95% CI coverage": f"{100 * cov_pr:.1f}%"},
])
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-se
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'The same 4,000 matched assignments as above, non-linear outcome. The two-sample standard error is calibrated to a design that was not run.'

se_tbl.style.hide(axis="index")
```

A two-sample $t$-test computes the standard error from the within-arm variances.
Under this design each arm contains one unit from every pair, so each arm spans
the full covariate range and its variance is close to the variance of the whole
sample. That calculation returns roughly the value it would have returned under
plain randomisation, while the estimate itself now moves around far less. The
interval is too wide by a factor of
`{python} f"{se_unpaired.mean() / sd_true:.2f}"`, and its coverage is
`{python} f"{100 * cov_un:.1f}"`% instead of 95%.

Differencing within pairs fixes it. The within-pair difference is the unit of
analysis, its spread already reflects how closely the pairs were matched, and
the resulting interval has
`{python} f"{100 * cov_pr:.1f}"`% coverage. A regression of the outcome on
treatment plus a fixed effect for each pair is the same calculation and gives
the same standard error. The cost is degrees of freedom, $N/2 - 1$ rather than
$N - 2$, which is minor at a few hundred units.

The upper bound on what this is worth is set by the covariates. For a perfectly
matched sample the variance of the estimate falls to the share of outcome
variance the covariates do not explain, so the naive variance is too large by at
most $1/(1 - R^2)$ and the naive standard error by at most
$1/\sqrt{1 - R^2}$. Here $R^2$ is
`{python} f"{r2_nl:.2f}"`, giving a ceiling of
`{python} f"{1 / (1 - r2_nl):.2f}"` on the variance and
`{python} f"{1 / np.sqrt(1 - r2_nl):.2f}"` on the standard error, against the
`{python} f"{(se_unpaired.mean() / sd_true) ** 2:.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{se_unpaired.mean() / sd_true:.2f}"` realised. Measured as variance
removed rather than as a ratio, the matching captured
`{python} f"{100 * (1 - sd_true ** 2 / se_unpaired.mean() ** 2) / r2_nl:.0f}"`%
of what a perfect matching would have removed.

### A conservative interval is not always a safe one

Calling the two-sample interval conservative is accurate but incomplete. It
does not follow that the only consequence is lost precision.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-power
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'Rejection rate of a two-sided 5% test against the size of the true effect, on the same sample. The matched design analysed without the pairing can be less powerful than not matching at all.'

taus = [0.0, 0.14, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55]
rows_p = []
for tau in taus:
    Yc = y_nl[None, :] + tau * T_cr
    a_ = np.where(T_cr, Yc, np.nan)
    b_ = np.where(T_cr, np.nan, Yc)
    e_c = np.nanmean(a_, 1) - np.nanmean(b_, 1)
    s_c = np.sqrt(np.nanvar(a_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2)
                  + np.nanvar(b_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2))
    pow_cr = (np.abs(e_c / s_c) > tc_un).mean()

    Yp = y_nl[None, :] + tau * T_pm
    a_ = np.where(T_pm, Yp, np.nan)
    b_ = np.where(T_pm, np.nan, Yp)
    e_p = np.nanmean(a_, 1) - np.nanmean(b_, 1)
    s_un = np.sqrt(np.nanvar(a_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2)
                   + np.nanvar(b_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2))
    wd = np.where(T_pm[:, i0], Yp[:, i0] - Yp[:, i1], Yp[:, i1] - Yp[:, i0])
    s_pr = wd.std(1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(nP)
    rows_p.append({
        "True effect": f"{tau:.2f}",
        "Plain randomisation": f"{100 * pow_cr:.0f}%",
        "Matched, two-sample SE": f"{100 * (np.abs(e_p / s_un) > tc_un).mean():.0f}%",
        "Matched, within-pair SE": f"{100 * (np.abs(e_p / s_pr) > tc_pr).mean():.0f}%",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows_p).style.hide(axis="index")
```

Read the middle column against the left one. At small effect sizes the matched
design analysed with a two-sample standard error rejects less often than plain
randomisation does, and the ordering only reverses once the effect is large
enough. A test statistic that is both smaller in spread and centred below the
critical value crosses that value less often, so the tighter estimate works
against you until the effect is big enough to clear the bar on its own. Bruhn
and McKenzie report the same effect: failing to account for the randomisation
method gives tests of the wrong size, and can give less power than a plain
random draw would have.

The right column is what the design was for.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The pairing has to survive to the analysis
Matching moves its gain into the analysis stage, where it needs the pair labels
to claim it. If the data reaches you aggregated, say a count and a sum per arm
per day, the pair structure is gone and the only standard error you can compute
is the conservative one. Store the pair identifier alongside the assignment at
the point you randomise, and carry it through every table that follows.

Rerandomization does not share this exposure, because a strict threshold banks
most of its gain at the design stage. If you know the analysis will run on
aggregates, that is a point in favour of a threshold over pairs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to do
Pair on the covariates you have reason to believe predict the outcome, solve
the matching exactly, keep the pair identifier, and analyse within pairs.
Matching on covariates that do not predict the outcome spends degrees of
freedom and returns nothing.
:::
